content: The International Code of Conduct on Pesticide Management – Guidance on Pesticide Legislation (Second Edition) was published in 2020 by the Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO) of the United Nations and the World Health Organization (WHO). This document provides comprehensive guidance on the development and implementation of pesticide legislation, aiming to ensure the safe and effective management of pesticides throughout their lifecycle. The designations and presentation of material in this publication do not imply any opinion by FAO or WHO regarding the legal or developmental status of any country, territory, or area, nor do they address the delimitation of boundaries. The mention of specific companies or products does not constitute endorsement or recommendation by FAO or WHO over others of a similar nature. The views expressed in this document are those of the authors and do not necessarily reflect the policies or positions of FAO or WHO. The Inter-Organization Programme for the Sound Management of Chemicals (IOMC) was established in 1995 to enhance international coordination in chemical safety. Participating organizations include FAO, WHO, the International Labour Organization (ILO), the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD), the United Nations Environment Programme (UNEP), the United Nations Industrial Development Organization (UNIDO), the United Nations Institute for Training and Research (UNITAR), and others. The IOMC aims to promote coordinated policies and activities for the sound management of chemicals, focusing on human health and environmental protection. The regulatory framework for pesticide control encompasses all legislation governing pesticide management, including environmental protection, public health, occupational health, water safety, food safety, wildlife conservation, and general chemical management. Pesticide legislation specifically refers to legal instruments designed to regulate pesticides, including primary laws and secondary regulations. The core of pesticide legislation is the primary law, which establishes principles, mandates, and responsibilities, often requiring parliamentary approval. Secondary legislation, such as regulations or decrees, provides detailed rules for implementing the primary law. Over the past 35 years, international and national legal frameworks for pesticide management have evolved significantly. The International Code of Conduct on the Distribution and Use of Pesticides was first adopted by FAO in 1985 and has since undergone several revisions to address emerging issues, including public health pesticides. In 2013, the Code was updated and renamed the International Code of Conduct on Pesticide Management. WHO adopted the Code in 2014 as its reference framework for international guidance on pesticide management. Several international agreements relevant to pesticide management have come into force since the Code's initial adoption. These include the Rotterdam Convention on the Prior Informed Consent Procedure for Certain Hazardous Chemicals and Pesticides in International Trade, the Stockholm Convention on Persistent Organic Pollutants, the Basel Convention on the Transboundary Movement of Hazardous Wastes, the Montreal Protocol on Substances that Deplete the Ozone Layer, and the ILO Convention on Safety and Health in Agriculture (C184). Other developments include the Strategic Approach to International Chemicals Management (SAICM) and the Globally Harmonized System of Classification and Labelling of Chemicals (GHS). At the time of the Code's first publication, many developing countries lacked pesticide legislation, and awareness of pesticide hazards was limited. Since then, significant progress has been made, with most countries now having some form of pesticide legislation. However, many existing laws have weaknesses, such as outdated penalties, unclear enforcement authority, or insufficient alignment with international agreements and regional initiatives. Institutional changes and new national legislation on environmental protection and chemical management may not have been adequately addressed. Governments regulate pesticides to protect human health and the environment from risks associated with pesticide use. This includes safeguarding pesticide users, consumers, crops, livestock, wildlife, and water bodies. Legislation also ensures the effectiveness of pesticide products and promotes fair markets for manufacturers, importers, and distributors. Comprehensive pesticide management requires a robust institutional infrastructure for registration, enforcement, and monitoring, as well as the promotion of Integrated Pest Management (IPM) and Integrated Vector Management (IVM). The Code of Conduct emphasizes that governments should consider local needs, social and economic conditions, literacy levels, climatic factors, and the availability of appropriate application equipment and personal protective equipment (PPE) when regulating pesticides. Monitoring pesticide use in local contexts can provide insights for further developing regulatory frameworks. Outdated national pesticide legislation may need to be revised to address new needs, issues, and international standards. Governments must also ensure that institutional responsibilities evolve to meet changing priorities and that information on hazards and risks is effectively disseminated. Finally, FAO and WHO provide technical guidelines and maintain a repository of national legislation relevant to pesticide management, which can serve as a reference for countries developing or updating their regulatory frameworks.
